claims.text: Rapid cooling minimizes interdiffusion at phase boundaries in multiphase eutectic high-entropy alloys.
Minimizing interdiffusion prevents depletion of corrosion-resistant elements at phase boundaries.
Rapidly cooled material retains greater local corrosion resistance when wear exposes phase boundaries at elevated temperature in a corrosive environment.
Slow cooling of a segregated multiphase AlCoCrFeNi eutectic HEA produces broad interphase diffusion zones.
Rapid cooling will produce sharper phase boundaries with smaller diffusion zones than conventional slow cooling.
Elemental gradients within slow-cooling-induced interphase diffusion zones cause local depletion of corrosion-resistant species.
Slow-cooled alloys exhibit significant phase-boundary interdiffusion under elevated-temperature mechanical wear.
Local depletion of corrosion-resistant elements weakens the corrosion resistance of interphase regions.
Wear removes surface layers and exposes compositionally weakened interphase regions.
Exposure of compositionally weakened interphase regions accelerates corrosion.
Rapid cooling suppresses phase-boundary interdiffusion and maintains corrosion-resistant boundary compositions during wear.
Relative to the slow-cooled baseline, rapid cooling will reduce the corrosion rate by roughly 20%.
Relative to the slow-cooled baseline, rapid cooling will improve wear resistance.
Relative to the slow-cooled baseline, rapid cooling will lower total coupled wear-corrosion degradation.
A comparison at approximately 350°C in chloride solution under identical controlled wear conditions can test the proposed processing–structure–degradation relationship.
Holding temperature, chloride environment, and wear conditions constant isolates interdiffusion from other degradation-influencing factors.
SEM-EDS can be used to compare phase-boundary sharpness and interphase elemental distributions before and after testing.

The hypothesis is falsified only if rapid cooling fails to create significantly sharper boundaries and the rapidly cooled samples fail to show statistically significant reductions in both corrosion rate and wear damage.
